  "text": "The laundrette was closing at six. At twenty past five, Ruth found a man's shirt turning alone in the last dryer.

She checked the basket beneath the folding table. Empty. Outside, a bus pulled away from the stop.

Her mother would have known whose shirt it was. She had known which customers wanted their collars pressed and which ones counted their change twice. Ruth had been running the place for eleven days.

At half past five, an elderly man came in carrying a shopping bag.

“I think I've left something,” he said.

Ruth pointed to the dryer.

He nodded but made no move towards it.

“Still damp?” he asked.

She opened the door and touched a cuff.

“No. It's ready.”

“Could it have another ten minutes?”

“It'll shrink.”

He looked at the chairs beside the window.

“My daughter finishes at six. She doesn't like me waiting outside her work.”

Ruth took the shirt out and laid it on the table.

“You can wait here.”

He sat, placing his bag between his shoes. A bunch of spring onions stuck out of the top.

She swept behind the machines. Then she wiped the powder from the soap drawer, a job she'd been avoiding all week.

“Your mother used to put the radio on,” he said.

“Where is it?”

“Under the counter.”

She found it beside a tin of buttons. The dial was fixed with tape.

At six, his daughter tapped on the glass. Ruth handed him the folded shirt.

“Same time Thursday?” he asked.

She glanced at the opening hours, then at the chairs.

“Yes,” she said. “We're open.”"
